title: Chapter 70 — The Sphynx
paragraphs: It should not have been omitted that before completely stripping the body of the whale, he was beheaded. Now, the beheading of the Sperm Whale is a scientific anatomical feat upon which experienced whale surgeons very much pride themselves — and not without reason.

Consider that the whale has nothing that can properly be called a neck. On the contrary, where his head and body seem to join, there, in that very place, is the thickest part of him. Remember also that the surgeon must operate from above, some eight or ten feet above his subject, and that the subject is almost hidden in a discolored, churning sea. Bear in mind, too, that under these untoward conditions he has to cut many feet deep into the flesh, and in that submerged tangle must feel after the joints and sever the head from the body at exactly the right point.

When first severed, the head is dropped astern and held there by a cable until the body is stripped. That done, if it belongs to a small whale, it is hoisted on deck to be dealt with at leisure. But with a full-grown whale, this is impossible. For the sperm whale's head makes up nearly one third of his entire bulk, and to completely suspend such a massive weight — even by the strongest tackle — would be to court the risk of pulling the masts from their sockets.

The Pequod's whale, being decapitated and the body stripped, the head was hoisted against the ship's side — about halfway out of the sea, so that it might still be partly supported by its native element. And there, with the strained craft steeply leaning over to it from the enormous downward drag, and every yard-arm tilted, and the masts whipped forward, you would almost think the ship herself was bowing in homage to the massive thing.

When this last task was done, it was noon, and the seamen went below to their dinner. Silence reigned over the previously tumultuous but now deserted deck. An intense copper calm, like a universal golden lotus, was more and more unfolding its noiseless, measureless petals upon the sea.

A short time passed, and up into this silence came Ahab, alone from his cabin. Taking a few turns on the quarterdeck, he paused to gaze over the side. Then slowly climbing into the main-chains, he took Stubb's long spade — still remaining there after the whale's decapitation — and striking it into the lower part of the half-suspended mass, he placed his foot upon it. From this position he could gaze almost directly into the whale's great divided head.

It was a black and hooded head. And hanging there in the midst of so intense a calm, it seemed the Sphinx's in the desert. "Speak, vast and venerable head," muttered Ahab, "which, though beardless, here and there looks hoary with moss. Speak, mighty head, and tell us the secret thing that is in you. Of all divers, you have dived the deepest. That head upon which the upper sun now gleams has moved amid the world's foundations. Where unrecorded names and navies rust, and untold hopes and anchors rot — where in her murderous hold this frigate earth is ballasted with bones of millions of the drowned — there, in that awful water-land, there was your most familiar home. You have been where bell or diver never went. You have slept by many a sailor's side, where sleepless mothers would give their lives to lay them down. You saw the locked lovers when leaping from their flaming ship, heart to heart they sank beneath the exulting wave. The true, the right worshippers of God — in their own eternal, living truth, the faithful ones — they have faced you, head, and gone down, giving no outcry. But you, vast, dark head — you are a Sphinx that will tell nothing."
"Sail ho!" cried a triumphant voice from the main-masthead.

"Aye? Well now, that's cheering," cried Ahab, suddenly straightening up, while whole thunderclouds swept aside from his brow. "That lively cry upon this deadly calm might almost convert a better man. — Where away?"
"Three points on the starboard bow, sir, and bringing down her breeze to us!"

"Better and better, man. Would that St. Paul would come along that way, and bring his breeze to my becalmed soul! O Nature, and O soul of man! How far beyond all speech are your linked parallels! Not the smallest atom stirs or lives in matter, but has its cunning counterpart in mind."
